title: Repeat speculations by the same speaker
note: One speculation per speaker per medium: when a speaker repeats a view about the same medium across works, the earliest counts; a speculation about a different medium counts separately. The others are kept here, off the wheel and out of every count, and are read in the speaker’s thread. Distinct speculations within one work (scenarios, concept cards, a workshop's statements) all count.

speculations.text: Books will soon be obsolete in the public schools. Scholars will be instructed through the eye. … Our school system will be completely changed inside of ten years.
speculations.speaker: Inventor
speculations.source: F. J. Smith, “The evolution of the motion picture: VI—Looking into the future with Thomas A. Edison,” New York Dramatic Mirror, vol. 70, no. 1803, p. 24, Jul. 9, 1913. [Online]. Available: Internet Archive

tetrad_detail.enhance: instruction, now “through the eye”, and a school system “completely changed”

speculations.text: I believe that the motion picture is destined to revolutionize our educational system and that in a few years it will supplant largely, if not entirely, the use of textbooks.
speculations.speaker: Inventor
speculations.source: H. Weir, “The story of the motion picture,” McClure’s Magazine, vol. 54, p. 85, Nov. 1922, as cited in L. Cuban, Teachers and Machines: The Classroom Use of Technology Since 1920. New York, NY, USA: Teachers College Press, 1986, p. 9.

tetrad_detail.enhance: the educational system, revolutionised by the motion picture

speculations.text: Textbooks as the principal medium of teaching will be as obsolete as the horse and carriage are now.
speculations.speaker: Inventor
speculations.source: H. Weir, “What Edison would like to do with the movies,” Collier’s, vol. 75, no. 8, pp. 20–21, Feb. 21, 1925. Compiled in “Thomas Edison’s education predictions,” muninn.net.

tetrad_detail.obsolesce: textbooks as the principal medium of teaching

speculations.text: There won’t be schools in the future. … I think the computer will blow up the school.
speculations.speaker: Researcher
speculations.source: S. Papert, 1984, as quoted in L. Cuban, Teachers and Machines: The Classroom Use of Technology Since 1920. New York, NY, USA: Teachers College Press, 1986, p. 72.

speculations.text: With AI, over the next decade, that will become free, commonplace — great medical advice, great tutoring.
speculations.speaker: Company
speculations.source: B. Gates, interview, The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, NBC, Feb. 2025, as reported by NBC and CNBC.

tetrad_detail.enhance: great tutoring, made free and commonplace
tetrad_detail.obsolesce: tutoring as a scarce, costly service

speculations.who: Seymour Papert, interviewed by David S. Bennahum
speculations.text: The power of computers is not to improve school but to replace it with a different kind of structure.
speculations.medium_wording: computers, above all in the home
speculations.speaker: Researcher
speculations.source: D. S. Bennahum, “School’s out? An interview with Seymour Papert,” MEME 2.13, 1996. [Online]. Republished on The Daily Papert.

tetrad_detail.obsolesce: school, replaced by “a different kind of structure”

speculations.text: I am convinced that education will undergo the kind of megachange that came in the wake of technological and scientific developments.
speculations.speaker: Researcher
speculations.source: S. Papert, “Why school reform is impossible,” J. Learning Sciences, vol. 6, no. 4, pp. 417–427, 1997.

speculations.text: Does the computer serve the curriculum or does it make it obsolete? … it makes it also obsolete.
speculations.speaker: Researcher
speculations.source: S. Papert, keynote address, presented at SqueakFest, 2006. Transcript on The Daily Papert.

speculations.text: Five years from now on the web for free you’ll be able to find the best lectures in the world. It will be better than any single university.
speculations.speaker: Company
speculations.source: B. Gates, remarks at the Techonomy Conf., Lake Tahoe, CA, USA, Aug. 6, 2010, as reported in TechCrunch, Aug. 6, 2010, and J. R. Young, The Chronicle of Higher Education, Aug. 9, 2010.

tetrad_detail.enhance: access to the best lectures in the world, for free
tetrad_detail.obsolesce: the university as the place to learn

speculations.who: Arthur Radebaugh, Closer Than We Think (Chicago Tribune)
speculations.text: Classroom automation may foreshadow an end to schoolhouses. … Lessons would be televised to students “going to school” at home, where their work would be done and transmitted to a control center for correction and grading.
speculations.medium_wording: Home learning console: an electronic desk receiving televised lessons and sending work to a control centre
speculations.speaker: Writer or artist
speculations.source: A. Radebaugh, Closer Than We Think [comic strip], Chicago Tribune, Dec. 18, 1960, as cited in M. Novak, “This computerized desk from the 1960s was going to let kids learn from home,” Paleofuture. Jun. 24, 2014. [Online]. Available: https://paleofuture.com/blog/2014/6/24/this-computerized-desk-from-the-1960s-was-going-to-let-kids-learn-from-home

tetrad_detail.enhance: schooling at home, with work graded remotely by a control centre
